questions.question: What is a big change happening in the car industry today?
options: Old engines are gone.
Cars are getting smaller.
Many new ideas are happening all at once.
Car prices are much lower.
questions.explanation: The text states that four major innovations (electrification, automation, shared mobility, connected mobility) are happening all at once, leading to big changes.

questions.question: Why are some car owners unhappy with their new cars?
options: Cars cost too much money.
Cars do not have simple features like smartphones.
Cars are too slow to drive.
Cars use too much fuel.
questions.explanation: Customers are dissatisfied because their vehicles lack the features and user-friendliness common in smartphones.

questions.question: What is a main idea behind a Software-Defined Vehicle (SDV)?
options: It is very fast to drive.
You can change its features easily with software.
It is cheaper to buy than other cars.
It has only one screen inside.
questions.explanation: An SDV is a car that is fully programmable, meaning new features can be developed and deployed through software.

questions.question: What happens to an SDV car over time?
options: It breaks down faster.
It uses more gas.
It gets better with new software updates.
It becomes impossible to fix.
questions.explanation: An SDV keeps getting better thanks to continuous delivery of new software features and updates throughout its lifetime.

questions.question: What is a big problem for car companies right now with software development?
options: Software is too cheap to make.
They use old ways to make software.
There is not enough software available.
Software makes cars too light.
questions.explanation: A hurdle is that developers cling to the software development methodologies of yesteryear.

questions.question: How often do traditional cars get big changes to their hardware and software systems?
options: Every month.
Every year.
About every seven years.
Never.
questions.explanation: Hardware and software in traditional cars are released simultaneously, meaning significant changes occur only once every seven years or so.

questions.question: What important lesson did car makers learn from what happened to Nokia and BlackBerry?
options: Phones are better than cars.
Old ways of working can cause companies to fail.
Making phones is easy.
Cars will soon fly.
questions.explanation: Nokia and BlackBerry were outpaced by smartphones, showing that relying on old business models can lead to failure.

questions.question: What does it mean to use a 'digital first' strategy for new cars?
options: Build the car first and then add digital features.
Sell digital products before selling cars.
Think about the user's digital experience first.
Only make cars that are fully digital.
questions.explanation: A 'digital first' strategy means starting with the digital customer experience and working backward to the solution designs.

questions.question: What is the main aim of an SDV becoming a 'habitat on wheels'?
options: To be a place for animals.
To be like a house that moves.
To use the car's unique parts for many new experiences.
To drive itself everywhere without a driver.
questions.explanation: A 'habitat on wheels' utilizes the specifics of the car to provide multisensory experiences that a smartphone could never match.

questions.question: What does 'cross-domain applications' mean in an SDV?
options: Applications that work in different countries.
Applications that only work on one part of the car.
Different car systems work together for one goal.
Applications that are very hard to make.
questions.explanation: Cross-domain experiences mean various vehicle functions and systems intercommunicate and interact harmoniously to enrich the overall journey.

questions.question: In the example of 'dog mode,' how does the car keep the dog safe?
options: It plays music for the dog.
It locks the doors tighter.
It uses the air conditioning and screens together.
It calls the owner automatically.
questions.explanation: The 'dog mode' example shows multiple systems like air conditioning, infotainment screen, and battery management working together.

questions.question: How much faster should new features for SDVs be developed compared to old ways?
options: 2 times faster.
5 times faster.
10 times faster.
100 times faster.
questions.explanation: The goal is a tenfold improvement over the old ways of delivering new features.

questions.question: How is the automotive industry different from the smartphone industry in terms of complexity?
options: Smartphones are more complex than cars.
Cars have many different, complex parts from different companies.
Cars are simpler to build than smartphones.
Cars have fewer software problems than smartphones.
questions.explanation: The automotive industry is still plagued by high levels of complexity and heterogeneity, with each subsystem often from a different vendor.

questions.question: Why is 'functional safety' a special concern for cars but not smartphones?
options: Cars are bigger than smartphones.
Cars are more fun to use.
Car systems can cause serious harm if they fail.
Smartphones do not have software.
questions.explanation: Unlike smartphones, vehicles are subject to stringent safety standards because malfunctions can have serious consequences.

questions.question: What does the ISO 26262 standard help with in car design?
options: To make cars look better.
To choose car colors.
To make sure car electrical systems are safe.
To decide car prices.
questions.explanation: ISO 26262 is a standard that deals with the functional safety of electrical and electronic systems within vehicles.

questions.question: Which part of a car would likely get a high ASIL rating, meaning it has a very high safety requirement?
options: The radio system.
The seat warmer.
The braking system.
The clock display.
questions.explanation: A safety-relevant function like a braking system would be assigned a high ASIL rating, requiring more rigorous safety standards.

questions.question: What is the 'clash of two worlds' problem for car makers?
options: Old cars versus new car designs.
Cars made in different countries.
Combining old ways of building cars with new software methods.
Drivers who like old cars versus those who like new cars.
questions.explanation: The 'clash of two worlds' refers to the challenge of merging the reliability of traditional engineering with the agility of modern software development.

questions.question: What must car companies change internally to build SDVs well?
options: Hire only new people for all jobs.
Use only one method for everything.
Let different teams work in different ways and at different speeds.
Stop making physical car parts entirely.
questions.explanation: OEMs must create organizations with suborganizations that can move at different speeds and work with different cultures, methods, and tools.

questions.question: How does a 'digital first' approach help test new car features?
options: It requires building many physical test cars.
It means less testing is needed overall.
It allows testing ideas virtually before building real parts.
It makes testing only for software bugs.
questions.explanation: Digital first means new ideas are explored in virtual environments, getting early user feedback long before any physical test vehicle is provided.

questions.question: How do SDVs help car manufacturers make better products after they are sold?
options: SDVs do not change after they are sold.
SDVs only fix problems when customers ask.
SDVs can measure how features are used to improve them.
SDVs send updates only once a year.
questions.explanation: SDVs can measure and assess actual usage of vehicle apps and features, allowing for data-driven improvement and innovations.
